pages.body_latex:
\chapter*{Unit 3A: Integral Foundations and Techniques}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Unit 3A: Integral Foundations and Techniques}

Differential calculus begins with a local question: how fast is a quantity changing right now? Integral calculus begins with the complementary question: if we know a rate, a density, or many tiny contributions, how much total change has accumulated?

This unit develops that question from the ground up. We begin with antiderivatives and simple total-change problems, then construct definite integrals from Riemann sums. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus reveals why accumulation and differentiation undo one another. The second half of the unit develops the standard computational techniques used in Calculus II: substitution, integration by parts, trigonometric methods, partial fractions, numerical integration, and improper integrals.

\begin{bgconcept}[title={The two central meanings of an integral}]
The symbol
\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
\]
can be read in two compatible ways:
\begin{enumerate}
\item as a limit of sums of small contributions \(f(x_i^*)\Delta x\); and
\item as the net accumulated change produced by the rate or density \(f\) from \(a\) to \(b\).
\end{enumerate}
The first meaning explains what the integral is. The Fundamental Theorem explains how antiderivatives compute it.
\end{bgconcept}

\section*{Unit map}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Antiderivatives and initial-value problems
\item Rates, accumulated change, and displacement
\item Partitions, sigma notation, and Riemann sums
\item The definite integral and its properties
\item The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
\item Basic antiderivative formulas and substitution
\item Integration by parts, trigonometric methods, and partial fractions
\item Numerical and improper integration
\item Reviews, cumulative practice, and two practice exams
\end{enumerate}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Why this is more than an area unit}]
Area is the most visible interpretation of a definite integral, but it is only one case. The same limiting process computes change from a rate, mass from density, work from variable force, probability from a density function, and many other totals. The common structure is not ``find an area.'' It is ``add continuously distributed contributions.''
\end{bgadvanced}

pages.title: Antiderivatives: Reversing a Derivative
pages.body_latex:
\section{Antiderivatives: Reversing a Derivative}
\lessonobjective{Recognize an antiderivative, verify one by differentiating, and explain why an entire family of antiderivatives differs by constants.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Why reversing a derivative is a new kind of problem}]
A derivative tells us how a function changes, but it deliberately forgets one piece of information: vertical position. Every function in the family \(F(x)+C\) has the same derivative because adding a constant shifts a graph without changing any of its slopes. Finding an antiderivative is therefore not the same as solving an ordinary algebra equation. We are recovering a whole family of possible original functions from their shared rate of change.

This reversal is the basic computational idea behind integral calculus. The fastest way to test an antiderivative is not to stare at it and hope; differentiate it. That verification habit matters because integration formulas are easier to misremember than derivative rules, and a thirty-second derivative check catches most errors immediately. Throughout this unit, every proposed antiderivative should be treated as a claim that can be verified rather than an answer that must be trusted.
\end{bgexposition}


\begin{bgexposition}[title={Start with a question you already know how to answer}]
Differentiation takes a function and produces its rate of change. Integral calculus frequently asks us to reverse that process. If a velocity is \(v(t)=6t-4\), which position functions could have produced it? Since
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(3t^2-4t)=6t-4,
\]
one answer is \(3t^2-4t\). But adding any constant leaves the derivative unchanged, so \(3t^2-4t+17\), \(3t^2-4t-200\), and infinitely many other functions work as well.
\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Antiderivative}]
A function \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) on an interval when
\[
F'(x)=f(x)
\]
for every \(x\) in that interval.
\end{bgdefinition}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Find and verify an antiderivative}]
Find an antiderivative of \(f(x)=4x^3-6x+5\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Reverse the power rule term by term:
\[
\int 4x^3\,dx=x^4,\qquad
\int -6x\,dx=-3x^2,\qquad
\int 5\,dx=5x.
\]
A candidate is
\[
F(x)=x^4-3x^2+5x.
\]
Differentiate to verify:
\[
F'(x)=4x^3-6x+5=f(x).
\]
Therefore \(F\) is an antiderivative.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Why the constant is unavoidable}]
If \(F'(x)=f(x)\), then \((F(x)+C)'=f(x)\) for every constant \(C\). Conversely, on a connected interval, any two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant. The derivative records slope, not vertical position.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-antiderivative-01}{expression}{2x^3-3x^2+4x+C}[Quick check]
Find the general antiderivative of \(6x^2-6x+4\).
\begin{bghint}Increase each power by one, divide by the new exponent, and include an arbitrary constant.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int(6x^2-6x+4)\,dx=2x^3-3x^2+4x+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Verify by differentiation that \(x^5/5\) is an antiderivative of \(x^4\).
\item Find the general antiderivative of \(3x^{-2}+2\sqrt{x}\).
\item Give two different antiderivatives of \(\cos x\).
\item Explain why no single number can be called ``the'' indefinite integral of a function without an initial condition.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Indefinite Integrals and the Constant of Integration
pages.body_latex:
\section{Indefinite Integrals and the Constant of Integration}
\lessonobjective{Use indefinite-integral notation correctly, distinguish an integrand from an antiderivative, and carry the constant of integration through calculations.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Reading indefinite-integral notation correctly}]
An indefinite integral is not a number and it is not an unfinished definite integral. It is a compact way to name all functions whose derivative equals the integrand. The symbol \(dx\) identifies the variable with respect to which the reversal is being performed, which becomes important when formulas contain several letters. The constant \(C\) records the vertical information that differentiation erased.

A useful discipline is to read \(\int f(x)\,dx\) aloud as ``the family of antiderivatives of \(f\) with respect to \(x\).'' That sentence makes several common mistakes harder to commit. It reminds us that \(+C\) belongs in an indefinite integral, that constants involving other fixed parameters remain constants, and that a final answer should differentiate back to the original integrand on the interval where the formula is intended to hold.
\end{bgexposition}


\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Indefinite integral}]
The notation
\[
\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C
\]
means that \(F'(x)=f(x)\). The function \(f\) is the \emph{integrand}, \(dx\) names the variable of integration, and \(C\) represents an arbitrary constant.
\end{bgdefinition}

The symbol \(\int\) is not a decorative elongated letter. It instructs us to collect the entire family of antiderivatives. Omitting \(+C\) changes a family into one member and loses information.

\begin{bgexample}[title={A fractional power}]
\[
\int \sqrt[3]{x^2}\,dx
=\int x^{2/3}\,dx
=\frac{x^{5/3}}{5/3}+C
=\frac35x^{5/3}+C.
\]
The derivative of \(\frac35x^{5/3}\) is \(x^{2/3}\), so the result checks.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={The exponent \(-1\) is the exception}]
The power rule for antiderivatives,
\[
\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,
\]
requires \(n\ne-1\). When \(n=-1\), the denominator \(n+1\) is zero. Instead,
\[
\int \frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+C.
\]
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-c-01}{expression}{-4/x+3x^2/2+C}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\int(4x^{-2}+3x)\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}For \(x^{-2}\), raise the exponent to \(-1\) and divide by \(-1\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int(4x^{-2}+3x)\,dx=-4x^{-1}+\frac32x^2+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Find \(\int(7-2x^4)\,dx\).
\item Find \(\int(5/x^3+e^x)\,dx\).
\item Explain why \(\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx\) does not require a \(+C\), while \(\int f(x)\,dx\) does.
\item Differentiate your answer to every computational exercise.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Initial-Value Problems and Recovering a Function
pages.body_latex:
\section{Initial-Value Problems and Recovering a Function}
\lessonobjective{Use a derivative or rate together with one known value to recover a unique function.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={How one measured value selects one function}]
An antiderivative gives a family because a derivative cannot tell where the original graph sits vertically. An initial condition supplies exactly that missing information. Once a rate law has been integrated, substituting one known function value turns the arbitrary constant into a specific number and selects one member of the family. This is why a velocity law alone does not determine position, while velocity together with one known position does.

The same pattern appears far beyond motion. A growth rate plus one measured population, a cooling rate plus one measured temperature, or a marginal cost plus one known total cost can each determine a unique model. The practical workflow is always the same: integrate the rate, introduce the constant, apply the known value, and then verify both the derivative relation and the initial condition. Skipping either verification leaves room for a model that is algebraically tidy but physically wrong.
\end{bgexposition}


An antiderivative family becomes one specific function after an initial condition fixes the vertical shift.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Recover a position function from velocity}]
A particle has velocity \(v(t)=6t-4\) meters per second and position \(s(2)=5\) meters. Find \(s(t)\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Since \(s'(t)=v(t)\), integrate:
\[
s(t)=3t^2-4t+C.
\]
Use the known position:
\[
5=s(2)=3(2)^2-4(2)+C=12-8+C=4+C.
\]
Therefore \(C=1\), and
\[
\boxed{s(t)=3t^2-4t+1}.
\]
Check: \(s'(t)=6t-4\), and \(s(2)=5\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgapplication}[title={A temperature model from a measured cooling rate}]
Suppose a sensor records a temperature-change rate \(T'(t)=-0.8e^{-0.2t}\) degrees Celsius per minute and \(T(0)=24\). Integration gives
\[
T(t)=4e^{-0.2t}+C.
\]
The initial value gives \(24=4+C\), so \(T(t)=20+4e^{-0.2t}\). The constant is not algebraic clutter; it identifies the ambient-temperature level approached by the model.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-ivp-01}{expression}{2x^3-x+4}[Quick check]
If \(F'(x)=6x^2-1\) and \(F(0)=4\), find \(F(x)\).
\begin{bghint}Integrate first, then substitute \(x=0\) to determine \(C\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[F(x)=2x^3-x+C,\quad F(0)=C=4.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item If \(y'=3x^2+2\) and \(y(1)=7\), find \(y\).
\item A car has acceleration \(a(t)=4t-2\), velocity \(v(0)=3\), and position \(s(0)=10\). Find \(v(t)\) and \(s(t)\).
\item Explain why one initial value determines one antiderivative constant but a second-order problem generally requires two initial values.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: From a Rate to Total Change
Displacement, Distance, and Signed Accumulation
pages.body_latex:
\section{Displacement, Distance, and Signed Accumulation}
\lessonobjective{Use the sign of velocity to distinguish displacement from total distance traveled.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Why signed accumulation and total travel differ}]
Velocity contains direction as well as speed. Positive velocity contributes positive displacement, while negative velocity contributes negative displacement. Consequently, \(\int_a^b v(t)\,dt\) records the net change in position: motion in opposite directions can cancel. A particle can travel a long way and still have zero displacement if it returns to its starting point.

Total distance asks a different question and therefore uses \(|v(t)|\). Before integrating for distance, locate every time at which velocity changes sign and split the interval there. This is not ceremonial bookkeeping. It prevents a segment traveled to the left from being subtracted from a segment traveled to the right, and it keeps the mathematical result aligned with the everyday meaning of distance traveled.
\end{bgexposition}


The integral of velocity gives displacement:
\[
\int_a^b v(t)\,dt=s(b)-s(a).
\]
If velocity is negative, the object moves in the negative direction and contributes negative displacement. Total distance ignores direction and instead uses speed:
\[
\text{distance}=\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt.
\]

\begin{bgexample}[title={A particle changes direction}]
Let \(v(t)=t-2\) on \([0,5]\). Then
\[
\int_0^5(t-2)\,dt=\left[\frac12t^2-2t\right]_0^5=\frac52.
\]
The displacement is \(2.5\). Since velocity changes sign at \(t=2\), total distance is
\[
-\int_0^2(t-2)\,dt+\int_2^5(t-2)\,dt=2+\frac92=\frac{13}{2}.
\]
The object ends \(2.5\) units to the right of its start after traveling \(6.5\) units in all.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-displacement-01}{integer}{0}[Quick check]
If \(v(t)=2t-4\) on \([0,4]\), what is the displacement?
\begin{bghint}Integrate the velocity over the full interval.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int_0^4(2t-4)\,dt=[t^2-4t]_0^4=0.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgmistake}
A negative definite integral does not mean negative distance. It means the net signed change points in the negative direction. Distance requires absolute value or interval-by-interval sign analysis.
\end{bgmistake}

pages.title: Partitions and Sigma Notation
pages.body_latex:
\section{Partitions and Sigma Notation}
\lessonobjective{Divide an interval into subintervals, calculate \(\Delta x\), and read or write finite sums in sigma notation.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Turning an interval into organized data}]
A partition is simply a list of points that cuts an interval into smaller subintervals. The widths need not be equal, although equal widths make many hand calculations easier. Once the pieces are named, sigma notation lets us describe repeated arithmetic without writing a page-long sum. The notation is compressed, but the underlying action is ordinary: evaluate, multiply by a width, and add.

Understanding the indices matters more than memorizing the symbol. The lower and upper limits of a sum tell us which terms are included, while the formula beside the sigma tells us how the \(i\)-th term is formed. In Riemann sums, the index connects each sample value to its corresponding subinterval width. A student who can expand a sigma expression into several concrete terms is far less likely to lose an endpoint or use the wrong number of rectangles.
\end{bgexposition}


A partition divides \([a,b]\) into smaller intervals. For \(n\) equal pieces,
\[
\Delta x=\frac{b-a}n,
\qquad x_i=a+i\Delta x.
\]
The symbol \(\sum\) compresses repeated addition:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Build a uniform partition}]
Partition \([1,5]\) into \(8\) equal subintervals.
\begin{bgsolution}
\[
\Delta x=\frac{5-1}8=\frac12.
\]
The endpoints are
\[
1,\frac32,2,\frac52,3,\frac72,4,\frac92,5.
\]
The right endpoint of subinterval \(i\) is \(x_i=1+i/2\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-partition-01}{rational}{3/5}[Quick check]
What is \(\Delta x\) when \([2,8]\) is divided into \(10\) equal subintervals?
\begin{bghint}Use \((b-a)/n\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\Delta x=(8-2)/10=3/5.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Expand \(\sum_{i=1}^4(2i-1)\).
\item Write \(3^2+4^2+5^2+6^2\) in sigma notation.
\item Find the left, right, and midpoint sample points for four equal subintervals of \([0,2]\).
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Left, Right, and Midpoint Riemann Sums
pages.body_latex:
\section{Left, Right, and Midpoint Riemann Sums}
\lessonobjective{Construct common Riemann sums, calculate them from formulas or tables, and reason about overestimates and underestimates.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Three reasonable approximations, three different biases}]
Left, right, and midpoint sums use the same partition but choose different representative heights. On an increasing function, left rectangles tend to lie below the graph and right rectangles tend to lie above it; for a decreasing function, the pattern reverses. Midpoint rectangles often balance some of that error because each height is sampled from the center rather than from one edge.

The point is not that one rule is always magically correct. The shape of the function and the fineness of the partition control the quality of the estimate. Before calculating, predict whether a rule should overestimate or underestimate. After calculating, compare the result with the graph and units. Numerical integration is most useful when it combines computation with a reasoned expectation about error.
\end{bgexposition}


On each subinterval, choose a sample point \(x_i^*\). The rectangle contribution is
\[
f(x_i^*)\Delta x.
\]
Adding gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\Delta x.
\]
Left sums use left endpoints, right sums use right endpoints, and midpoint sums use subinterval midpoints.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Three estimates for one integral}]
Estimate the area under \(f(x)=x^2+1\) on \([0,2]\) using four rectangles.
\begin{bgsolution}
Here \(\Delta x=1/2\).

Left endpoints: \(0,1/2,1,3/2\):
\[
L_4=\frac12\left(1+\frac54+2+\frac{13}4\right)=\frac{15}{4}.
\]
Right endpoints: \(1/2,1,3/2,2\):
\[
R_4=\frac12\left(\frac54+2+\frac{13}4+5\right)=\frac{23}{4}.
\]
Midpoints: \(1/4,3/4,5/4,7/4\):
\[
M_4=\frac12\left(\frac{17}{16}+\frac{25}{16}+\frac{41}{16}+\frac{65}{16}\right)=\frac{37}{8}.
\]
Because \(f\) is increasing, the left sum underestimates and the right sum overestimates.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-riemann-01}{integer}{5}[Quick check]
Use two left-endpoint rectangles to approximate \(\int_0^2 (x+2)\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}Each subinterval has width 1. Use heights \(f(0)\) and \(f(1)\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[L_2=1\bigl(f(0)+f(1)\bigr)=2+3=5.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: The Riemann-Sum Definition of the Definite Integral
pages.body_latex:
\section{The Riemann-Sum Definition of the Definite Integral}
\lessonobjective{Explain the definite integral as a limit and translate between sigma and integral notation.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={From rectangles to an exact total}]
A single Riemann sum is an approximation because each rectangle replaces a varying function by one constant height. The definite integral is obtained by considering a sequence of finer partitions whose largest subinterval width approaches zero. If all valid choices of sample points lead to the same limiting value, that value is the integral. The exact total is therefore defined by the stability of increasingly detailed approximations.

This definition explains why the integral is more general than a geometric area formula. The terms may represent signed change, mass, probability, or any other continuously distributed contribution. It also explains why integrability is a mathematical condition rather than a drawing convention: the sums must settle toward one value. Continuous functions on closed intervals satisfy this requirement, giving us a large and reliable class of integrable functions.
\end{bgexposition}


\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Definite integral}]
If the limit exists and is independent of the sample points,
\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\Delta x.
\]
\end{bgdefinition}

The integral is one number. The Riemann sums are approximations indexed by \(n\). As the largest subinterval width approaches zero, the approximations converge to the integral.

\begin{bgexample}[title={Evaluate \(\int_0^1 x\,dx\) from the definition}]
Use right endpoints with \(\Delta x=1/n\) and \(x_i=i/n\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i}{n}\frac1n
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n i
=\frac1{n^2}\frac{n(n+1)}2
=\frac{n+1}{2n}.
\]
Taking the limit gives
\[
\int_0^1x\,dx=\frac12.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Integrability is a theorem, not a visual promise}]
Continuous functions on closed intervals are Riemann integrable. Many discontinuous functions are also integrable, but not every bounded function is. A later analysis course makes precise how the set and severity of discontinuities control Riemann integrability.
\end{bgadvanced}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-riemann-limit-01}{rational}{1/2}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n}\).
\begin{bghint}Divide numerator and denominator by \(n\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\frac{1+1/n}{2}\to\frac12.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: The Definite Integral as Signed Area
Properties and Orientation of Definite Integrals
pages.body_latex:
\section{Properties and Orientation of Definite Integrals}
\lessonobjective{Use linearity, interval additivity, comparison, and reversed limits without unnecessary computation.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Integral properties reflect how accumulation behaves}]
The algebraic properties of definite integrals are not arbitrary rules. Linearity says that scaling or combining rates scales or combines their accumulated effects. Additivity says that accumulating from \(a\) to \(c\) and then from \(c\) to \(b\) gives the same total as accumulating directly from \(a\) to \(b\). Reversing the bounds changes the sign because it reverses the orientation of the accumulation.

These properties are computational tools as well as conceptual checks. They let us reconstruct an unknown integral from known pieces, compare integrals without finding antiderivatives, and detect impossible answers. For example, if \(f\ge0\) on an interval, its integral cannot be negative. A strong solution uses such facts before and after computation rather than treating the evaluation formula as the only source of truth.
\end{bgexposition}


For integrable functions,
\[
\int_a^a f=0,
\qquad
\int_b^a f=-\int_a^b f,
\]
\[
\int_a^b(cf+g)=c\int_a^bf+\int_a^bg,
\]
and for \(a<c<b\),
\[
\int_a^b f=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f.
\]
If \(m\le f(x)\le M\) on \([a,b]\), then
\[
m(b-a)\le\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\le M(b-a).
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Use known integrals}]
Suppose \(\int_0^2 f=3\) and \(\int_2^5f=-4\). Find \(\int_5^0(2f+1)\,dx\).
\begin{bgsolution}
First,
\[
\int_0^5f=3+(-4)=-1,
\qquad
\int_5^0f=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_5^0(2f+1)\,dx=2(1)+(0-5)=-3.
\]
The integral of \(1\) from \(5\) to \(0\) is \(-5\), because orientation matters.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-properties-01}{integer}{-7}[Quick check]
If \(\int_1^4 f=7\), what is \(\int_4^1 f\)?
\begin{bghint}Reversing limits changes the sign.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int_4^1 f=-7.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Average Value of a Function
Accumulation Functions
pages.body_latex:
\section{Accumulation Functions}
\lessonobjective{Interpret a variable-upper-limit integral as a new function and reason about its increase, decrease, and units.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={An integral can define a new function}]
When the upper limit varies, \(A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) records how much signed accumulation has occurred by the time the input reaches \(x\). The dummy variable \(t\) is used inside the integral so that \(x\) can remain free to control the endpoint. As \(x\) moves, the accumulated region grows, shrinks, or gains negative contribution depending on the sign of \(f\).

The graph of \(A\) can often be predicted directly from the graph of \(f\). Where \(f\) is positive, \(A\) increases; where \(f\) is negative, \(A\) decreases; where \(f=0\), \(A\) has a horizontal tangent. This makes accumulation functions a bridge between geometric area, net change, and derivative behavior, setting up the Fundamental Theorem rather than appearing as an isolated notation trick.
\end{bgexposition}


Fix a starting point \(a\) and define
\[
A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt.
\]
The variable \(t\) is a dummy variable inside the integral; \(x\) determines where accumulation stops.

If \(f>0\), moving \(x\) to the right adds positive contributions and \(A\) increases. If \(f<0\), \(A\) decreases. The value \(A(x)\) is a total; the value \(f(x)\) is the local rate at which that total changes.

\begin{bgexample}[title={Build an accumulation function directly}]
For \(f(t)=2t\) and \(a=1\),
\[
A(x)=\int_1^x2t\,dt=x^2-1.
\]
Thus \(A(1)=0\), \(A(2)=3\), and \(A'(x)=2x=f(x)\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-accumulation-01}{integer}{0}[Quick check]
For \(A(x)=\int_3^x f(t)\,dt\), what is \(A(3)\)?
\begin{bghint}The interval has zero width.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[A(3)=\int_3^3f(t)\,dt=0.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part I
pages.body_latex:
\section{Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part I}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate accumulation functions and explain why the derivative recovers the integrand.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Why the derivative of accumulated area returns the integrand}]
Suppose \(A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\). Increasing \(x\) by a small amount \(h\) adds a thin strip whose width is \(h\) and whose height is close to \(f(x)\). The added accumulation is therefore approximately \(f(x)h\), so the quotient \([A(x+h)-A(x)]/h\) is approximately \(f(x)\). In the limit, the approximation becomes exact under the theorem's hypotheses.

This result is profound because it says accumulation has a local rate, and that rate is precisely the function being accumulated. It is the mathematical statement that a running total changes at the current input rate. The theorem turns area and accumulation functions into differentiable objects and explains why integration and differentiation are inverse processes rather than unrelated chapters placed next to each other by tradition.
\end{bgexposition}


\begin{bgtheorem}[title={FTC Part I}]
If \(f\) is continuous and
\[
A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt,
\]
then
\[
A'(x)=f(x).
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

Why? Increasing \(x\) by a small amount \(h\) adds a thin strip whose width is \(h\) and whose height is approximately \(f(x)\). Thus
\[
\frac{A(x+h)-A(x)}h
=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt
\approx f(x).
\]
The approximation becomes exact in the limit.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate without evaluating the integral}]
If
\[
G(x)=\int_2^x\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{G'(x)=\sqrt{1+x^4}}.
\]
No elementary antiderivative is needed.
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-ftc1-01}{expression}{cos(x^2)}[Quick check]
If \(F(x)=\int_0^x\cos(t^2)\,dt\), find \(F'(x)\).
\begin{bghint}FTC Part I returns the integrand evaluated at the upper bound.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[F'(x)=\cos(x^2).\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Continuity is sufficient, not the final word}]
FTC Part I is commonly stated for continuous integrands because that hypothesis is easy to check and strong enough for a clean theorem. More advanced integration theories weaken the hypotheses and clarify exactly where the derivative of an accumulation function exists.
\end{bgadvanced}

pages.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part II
The Net Change Theorem
pages.body_latex:
\section{The Net Change Theorem}
\lessonobjective{Translate a contextual rate integral into final amount minus initial amount.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Rates become measurable changes}]
If \(Q'(t)\) is the rate at which a quantity changes, then \(\int_a^b Q'(t)\,dt=Q(b)-Q(a)\). This net-change statement is the Fundamental Theorem written in applied language. It tells us that integrating a rate over time recovers the actual change in the underlying quantity, whether that quantity is position, volume, charge, population, energy, or cost.

The word ``net'' matters whenever the rate can be negative. Inflow and outflow, charging and discharging, or forward and backward motion contribute with opposite signs. To recover the final amount, add the net change to the initial amount. To recover total activity without cancellation, a different model may be needed, often involving absolute value or separate positive and negative contributions.
\end{bgexposition}


If \(Q'(t)\) is a rate of change, then
\[
\int_a^bQ'(t)\,dt=Q(b)-Q(a).
\]
This is FTC Part II interpreted in context.

\begin{bgapplication}[title={Charge flowing through a circuit}]
Current \(I(t)\), measured in amperes, is charge flow in coulombs per second. If
\[
I(t)=3e^{-t}+1
\]
for \(0\le t\le4\), then the net charge transferred is
\[
\int_0^4I(t)\,dt=[-3e^{-t}+t]_0^4=7-3e^{-4}\text{ coulombs}.
\]
The units make the interpretation unavoidable: amperes times seconds equals coulombs.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-net-change-01}{integer}{24}[Quick check]
A population changes at rate \(P'(t)=3t\) people/year for \(0\le t\le4\). What is the net population change?
\begin{bghint}Integrate the rate over the time interval.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int_0^4 3t\,dt=\frac32(16)=24.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Variable Limits and the Chain Rule
pages.body_latex:
\section{Variable Limits and the Chain Rule}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate integrals whose bounds are functions of the differentiation variable.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={An accumulation endpoint can itself be changing}]
The Fundamental Theorem handles \(\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\), but many problems use an endpoint such as \(g(x)\). In that case the accumulated total changes for two reasons: the endpoint moves, and the speed of that movement is \(g'(x)\). The derivative is therefore \(f(g(x))g'(x)\), which is the ordinary chain rule applied to an accumulation function.

Lower limits contribute a minus sign because moving the lower endpoint to the right removes accumulation rather than adding it. With both endpoints variable, differentiate the upper contribution and subtract the lower contribution. A reliable approach is to name the accumulation function first, apply the Fundamental Theorem, and then apply the chain rule visibly rather than attempting to remember a pile of signs from memory.
\end{bgexposition}


If
\[
G(x)=\int_a^{g(x)}f(t)\,dt,
\]
then
\[
G'(x)=f(g(x))g'(x).
\]
The FTC supplies the outer derivative; the chain rule supplies the factor \(g'(x)\).

If both limits vary,
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)\,dt
=f(v(x))v'(x)-f(u(x))u'(x).
\]

\begin{bgexample}[title={Two moving boundaries}]
For
\[
H(x)=\int_{x^2}^{\sin x}e^{t^2}\,dt,
\]
\[
H'(x)=e^{\sin^2x}\cos x-e^{x^4}(2x).
\]
No elementary antiderivative of \(e^{t^2}\) is required.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-variable-limits-01}{expression}{2x*sin(x^2)}[Quick check]
Find \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^{x^2}\sin t\,dt\).
\begin{bghint}Evaluate the integrand at \(x^2\), then multiply by \(2x\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[2x\sin(x^2).\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Basic Antiderivative Rules
pages.body_latex:
\section{Basic Antiderivative Rules}
\lessonobjective{Use the standard power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric antiderivative formulas.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Integration rules are derivative rules read backward}]
The basic antiderivative table is built from familiar derivatives. Powers, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions are integrated by asking which function differentiates to the given integrand. This reverse-recognition viewpoint is more durable than treating the table as a disconnected list. It also makes verification immediate: differentiate the proposed answer.

Reverse rules require attention to constants and domains. A coefficient may need to be divided out, the power rule excludes exponent \(-1\), and \(\int 1/x\,dx\) requires \(\ln|x|\). No basic table can replace algebraic simplification. Rewriting radicals and reciprocals as powers often reveals that a seemingly new integral is simply an old rule in less cooperative clothing.
\end{bgexposition}


For \(n\ne-1\),
\[
\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C.
\]
Other central formulas include
\[
\int e^x\,dx=e^x+C,
\qquad
\int\frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+C,
\]
\[
\int\cos x\,dx=\sin x+C,
\qquad
\int\sin x\,dx=-\cos x+C,
\]
\[
\int\sec^2x\,dx=\tan x+C,
\qquad
\int\frac1{1+x^2}\,dx=\arctan x+C.
\]

\begin{bgdecision}[title={Normalize before integrating}]
Rewrite roots as fractional powers, move denominator powers into negative exponents when helpful, split sums, and factor out constants. Integration is often easy after the algebra stops wearing a disguise.
\end{bgdecision}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-basic-rules-01}{expression}{x^4/4-2cos(x)+C}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\int(x^3+2\sin x)\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}Integrate each term and remember that the antiderivative of sine is negative cosine.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[x^4/4-2\cos x+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Substitution: Reversing the Chain Rule
pages.body_latex:
\section{Substitution: Reversing the Chain Rule}
\lessonobjective{Recognize chain-rule structure, choose a useful substitution, transform the differential, and return to the original variable.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Substitution reverses the chain rule}]
A composite derivative has the pattern \(F'(g(x))g'(x)\). Substitution recognizes that pattern inside an integral, names the inner expression \(u=g(x)\), and replaces the accompanying derivative factor with \(du\). The purpose is not to change letters for entertainment; it is to turn a complicated composite integrand into a basic antiderivative in one variable.

A good substitution accounts for every factor, including the differential. After choosing \(u\), compute \(du\) explicitly and compare it with what remains in the integrand. Constant multiples can be adjusted, but missing variable factors cannot be wished into existence. For an indefinite integral, return to the original variable at the end and verify by differentiating through the chain rule.
\end{bgexposition}


The chain rule says
\[
\frac{d}{dx}F(g(x))=F'(g(x))g'(x).
\]
Reversing it gives
\[
\int F'(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=F(g(x))+C.
\]
The notation \(u=g(x)\), \(du=g'(x)\,dx\) organizes this reversal.

\begin{bgguided}[title={A complete substitution}]
Evaluate
\[
\int 2x(x^2+5)^7\,dx.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Choose the inner expression:
\[
u=x^2+5,
\qquad du=2x\,dx.
\]
Then
\[
\int 2x(x^2+5)^7\,dx=\int u^7\,du=\frac{u^8}8+C.
\]
Return to \(x\):
\[
\boxed{\frac{(x^2+5)^8}8+C}.
\]
Differentiate to check; the chain rule restores the missing \(2x\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-substitution-01}{expression}{(3x+1)^5/15+C}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\int(3x+1)^4\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}Let \(u=3x+1\), so \(du=3dx\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\frac13\int u^4du=\frac{u^5}{15}+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgmistake}
A substitution is incomplete if both \(x\) and \(u\) remain in the transformed integral. Every factor must be rewritten or accounted for before integration.
\end{bgmistake}

pages.title: Definite Integrals by Substitution
Integration by Parts
pages.body_latex:
\section{Integration by Parts}
\lessonobjective{Derive the formula from the product rule, choose \(u\) and \(dv\), and use the method on products and disguised products.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Integration by parts redistributes a product}]
Integration by parts comes from integrating the product rule. It is useful when an integrand is a product whose factors become easier in different directions: one factor simplifies when differentiated, while the other can be integrated. The formula \(\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du\) does not eliminate work automatically; it trades the original integral for a hopefully simpler one.

Choosing \(u\) and \(dv\) is therefore the central judgment. Logarithmic and inverse-trigonometric factors are usually chosen as \(u\) because they are difficult to integrate directly but manageable to differentiate. Polynomial factors often improve when differentiated. After applying the formula, compare the new integral with the old one. If it is more complicated, reconsider the choice rather than marching deeper into algebraic wilderness out of loyalty to the first idea.
\end{bgexposition}


From the product rule,
\[
(uv)'=u'v+uv'.
\]
Integrating and rearranging gives
\[
\boxed{\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du}.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Polynomial times exponential}]
Evaluate \(\int xe^x\,dx\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Choose \(u=x\), so \(du=dx\). Choose \(dv=e^x dx\), so \(v=e^x\). Then
\[
\int xe^x\,dx=xe^x-\int e^x\,dx=xe^x-e^x+C.
\]
Factor if desired:
\[
e^x(x-1)+C.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A disguised product}]
To integrate \(\ln x\), write \(\ln x\cdot1\). Let \(u=\ln x\) and \(dv=dx\). Then
\[
\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-\int1\,dx=x\ln x-x+C.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-parts-01}{expression}{xe^x-e^x+C}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\int xe^x\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}Let \(u=x\) and \(dv=e^x dx\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[xe^x-e^x+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Trigonometric Integrals
Trigonometric Substitution
pages.body_latex:
\section{Trigonometric Substitution}
\lessonobjective{Match radical patterns to trigonometric identities and return to the original variable using a reference triangle.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Use a trigonometric identity to simplify a radical}]
Expressions such as \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\), \(\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\), and \(\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\) resemble the Pythagorean identities for sine, tangent, and secant. Trigonometric substitution chooses a new variable so that the radical collapses to a simpler trigonometric expression. The method is less about trigonometry itself than about replacing a difficult algebraic geometry with a familiar right-triangle identity.

The substitution must respect the domain and the sign of the square root. Drawing a reference triangle makes the return to \(x\) concrete and prevents inverse-trigonometric confusion. Because this method can create substantial algebra, it should not be the first reflex for every radical. Simplify first and check whether an ordinary substitution is available before deploying the full trigonometric apparatus.
\end{bgexposition}


Standard patterns are:
\[
\sqrt{a^2-x^2}:\ x=a\sin\theta,
\qquad
\sqrt{a^2+x^2}:\ x=a\tan\theta,
\qquad
\sqrt{x^2-a^2}:\ x=a\sec\theta.
\]
The substitutions are chosen because \(1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\), \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\), and \(\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta\).

\begin{bgexample}[title={A circular radical}]
Evaluate
\[
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}.
\]
Let \(x=3\sin\theta\), so \(dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{9-x^2}=3\cos\theta\) on the chosen interval. Then
\[
\int d\theta=\theta+C=\arcsin(x/3)+C.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-trig-sub-01}{multiple_choice}{x=5tan(theta)}[Quick check]
Which substitution is natural for \(\sqrt{x^2+25}\)?
\begin{bghint}Match \(x^2+a^2\) to \(1+\tan^2\theta\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}Use \(x=5\tan\theta\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Partial Fractions
pages.body_latex:
\section{Partial Fractions}
\lessonobjective{Decompose proper rational functions and integrate linear and repeated-linear terms.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Turn one rational function into several familiar ones}]
Partial fractions is an algebraic decomposition used before integration. A proper rational function with a factorable denominator can often be written as a sum of simpler fractions whose antiderivatives are logarithmic or arctangent forms. The calculus step is usually easy once the decomposition is correct; most errors originate in incomplete factoring or an incorrect template.

Begin by performing polynomial division if the numerator's degree is not smaller than the denominator's. Then factor over the real numbers and include the correct terms for repeated linear factors and irreducible quadratics. Solve for the coefficients, integrate term by term, and differentiate or recombine the result as a check. Treating the algebra as part of the method, rather than as preliminary clutter, makes the procedure far more reliable.
\end{bgexposition}


When a rational function is proper and the denominator factors, rewrite it as a sum of simpler fractions.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Two distinct linear factors}]
Evaluate
\[
\int\frac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Write
\[
\frac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}.
\]
Then
\[
5x+1=A(x+2)+B(x-1).
\]
Setting \(x=1\) gives \(6=3A\), so \(A=2\). Setting \(x=-2\) gives \(-9=-3B\), so \(B=3\). Therefore
\[
\int\left(\frac2{x-1}+\frac3{x+2}\right)dx
=2\ln|x-1|+3\ln|x+2|+C.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmethod}[title={Before decomposing}]
If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, perform polynomial division first. Then factor the denominator completely over the real numbers and include the correct form for repeated or irreducible quadratic factors.
\end{bgmethod}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-pf-01}{expression}{ln|x|-ln|x+1|+C}[Quick check]
Evaluate \(\int \frac{1}{x(x+1)}\,dx\).
\begin{bghint}Decompose as \(1/x-1/(x+1)\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\ln|x|-\ln|x+1|+C.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Choosing an Integration Strategy
Midpoint and Trapezoidal Rules
Simpson’s Rule
Improper Integrals over Infinite Intervals
pages.body_latex:
\section{Improper Integrals over Infinite Intervals}
\lessonobjective{Replace an infinite bound by a limit and determine convergence or divergence.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Infinity enters through a limit, not as an endpoint number}]
An integral such as \(\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx\) is defined by replacing infinity with a finite boundary \(b\), evaluating \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), and then taking the limit as \(b\to\infty\). The integral converges only if that limit exists and is finite. We never substitute infinity into an antiderivative as though it were an oversized real number.

Convergence depends on the long-run balance between interval length and function decay. A positive function may approach zero and still have an infinite total area if it decays too slowly. The classic \(p\)-integrals show the threshold clearly. This distinction becomes important in probability, physics, and series theory, where an infinite domain can still carry a finite total mass or energy.
\end{bgexposition}


Define
\[
\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_a^bf(x)\,dx,
\]
provided the limit exists and is finite.

\begin{bgexample}[title={A convergent tail}]
\[
\int_1^\infty\frac1{x^2}\,dx
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac1x\right]_1^b
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left(1-\frac1b\right)=1.
\]
Although the interval is infinite, the tail contributions shrink fast enough to produce a finite total.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A divergent tail}]
\[
\int_1^\infty\frac1x\,dx
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\ln b=\infty.
\]
The integral diverges.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3a-improper-inf-01}{multiple_choice}{converges}[Quick check]
Does \(\int_1^\infty x^{-3}\,dx\) converge or diverge?
\begin{bghint}Use the p-integral threshold: \(p>1\) converges.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}It converges, with value \(1/2\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Improper Integrals with Unbounded Integrands
Unit 3A Review: Integral Foundations and Techniques
pages.body_latex:
\section{Unit 3A Review}
\begin{bgsummary}[title={Core ideas}]
\begin{itemize}
\item Antiderivatives reverse differentiation and form families differing by constants.
\item Riemann sums approximate continuously distributed totals.
\item Definite integrals are signed accumulations and limits of Riemann sums.
\item The Fundamental Theorem links differentiation and integration.
\item Substitution reverses the chain rule; integration by parts reverses the product rule.
\item Numerical methods estimate integrals when exact antiderivatives are unavailable.
\item Improper integrals are defined by limits and may converge or diverge.
\end{itemize}
\end{bgsummary}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Find \(\int(3x^2-4/x+\cos x)dx\).
\item Approximate \(\int_0^2e^{-x^2}dx\) using four midpoint rectangles.
\item Differentiate \(F(x)=\int_1^{x^3}\ln(1+t^2)dt\).
\item Evaluate \(\int_0^1x(1+x^2)^5dx\).
\item Evaluate \(\int x\cos x\,dx\).
\item Evaluate \(\int\frac{3x+5}{x^2+5x+6}dx\) by partial fractions.
\item Determine convergence of \(\int_2^\infty x^{-3/2}dx\).
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Common Integral Errors and How to Repair Them
pages.body_latex:
\section{Common Integral Errors}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Forgetting \(+C\) on indefinite integrals.
\item Adding \(+C\) to a definite integral.
\item Treating signed area as total geometric area.
\item Using \(u\)-integrands with unchanged \(x\)-bounds.
\item Applying the power rule to \(x^{-1}\).
\item Choosing integration by parts when simple algebra or substitution works first.
\item Crossing a singularity without splitting an improper integral.
\item Trusting an antiderivative without differentiating it.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3A Cumulative Practice
pages.body_latex:
\section{Cumulative Practice}
\begin{bgexercises}
\item Find the antiderivative family for \(5x^4-3x^{-2}+2e^x\).
\item Recover \(F\) if \(F'(x)=\sin x+x^2\) and \(F(0)=5\).
\item Construct \(L_4,R_4,M_4\) for \(f(x)=1/x\) on \([1,3]\).
\item Evaluate \(\int_{-2}^2(x^3+4)dx\) by symmetry and FTC.
\item Find the average value of \(x^2\) on \([0,3]\).
\item Differentiate \(\int_{\cos x}^{x^2}\sqrt{1+t^4}dt\).
\item Evaluate \(\int 4x e^{2x^2}dx\).
\item Evaluate \(\int x^2\ln x\,dx\).
\item Evaluate \(\int\sin^3x\cos^4x\,dx\).
\item Evaluate \(\int dx/(x^2-1)\) on an interval avoiding the singularities.
\item Approximate \(\int_0^2\sqrt{1+x^3}dx\) by the trapezoidal rule with \(n=4\).
\item Determine whether \(\int_0^1x^{-4/5}dx\) converges.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Unit 3A Practice Exam A
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam A}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Evaluate
\[
\int\left(4x^3-\frac{2}{x}+\sec^2x\right)\,dx.
\]
\item Use four midpoint rectangles to estimate
\[
\int_0^2(x^2+1)\,dx.
\]
Show the subinterval width and the four midpoint sample values.
\item Explain the difference between an indefinite integral and a definite integral. Your answer must mention both the type of output and the role of the constant of integration.
\item Differentiate
\[
G(x)=\int_1^{\sin x}e^{t^2}\,dt.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int_0^1 2x(1+x^2)^4\,dx.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int xe^{2x}\,dx.
\]
\item Evaluate by partial fractions:
\[
\int\frac{3x+5}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx.
\]
\item Determine whether
\[
\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx
\]
converges. If it converges, find its value. Show the limit that defines the improper integral.
\item A tank's net inflow rate is \(r(t)\) liters per minute. Explain the meaning and units of
\[
\int_0^5r(t)\,dt.
\]
State how a negative value should be interpreted.
\item Compare midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson estimates. State one reason Simpson's Rule is often more accurate for a smooth function and one reason no numerical estimate should be accepted without a reasonableness check.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3A Practice Exam A Answer Key
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam A Answer Key}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\[
\int\left(4x^3-\frac2x+\sec^2x\right)dx
=x^4-2\ln|x|+\tan x+C.
\]
\item Here \(\Delta x=\tfrac12\) and the midpoints are \(\tfrac14,\tfrac34,\tfrac54,\tfrac74\). Thus
\[
M_4=\frac12\left[\left(\frac1{16}+1\right)+\left(\frac9{16}+1\right)+\left(\frac{25}{16}+1\right)+\left(\frac{49}{16}+1\right)\right]
=\frac{37}{8}.
\]
\item An indefinite integral is a family of antiderivatives and therefore includes \(+C\). A definite integral is a number defined by a limit of sums; it has fixed bounds and no arbitrary \(+C\) in the final value.
\item By the Fundamental Theorem and chain rule,
\[
G'(x)=e^{\sin^2x}\cos x.
\]
\item Let \(u=1+x^2\), so \(du=2x\,dx\), and change the bounds from \(x=0,1\) to \(u=1,2\):
\[
\int_1^2u^4du=\left[\frac{u^5}{5}\right]_1^2=\frac{31}{5}.
\]
\item With \(u=x\), \(dv=e^{2x}dx\), and \(v=\tfrac12e^{2x}\),
\[
\int xe^{2x}dx=\frac{x e^{2x}}2-\frac{e^{2x}}4+C.
\]
\item Since
\[
\frac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac2{x+1}+\frac1{x+2},
\]
we get
\[
2\ln|x+1|+\ln|x+2|+C.
\]
\item
\[
\int_1^\infty\frac1{x^2}dx
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac1x\right]_1^b
=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left(1-\frac1b\right)=1.
\]
The integral converges.
\item The integral is the net change in the amount of water from time 0 to 5 minutes, measured in liters. A negative value means the tank lost more water than it gained over the interval.
\item Midpoint and trapezoidal rules use constant or linear local approximations; Simpson's Rule uses quadratic pieces and is often more accurate for smooth functions. Every estimate must still be checked against sign, rough area, monotonicity, and a reasonable magnitude.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3A Practice Exam B
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam B}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Evaluate
\[
\int\left(3x^{-1/2}+4e^x-5\cos x\right)\,dx.
\]
\item Use four right-endpoint rectangles to estimate
\[
\int_0^2x^2\,dx.
\]
\item Find the average value of \(f(x)=x^2+1\) on \([0,3]\).
\item Differentiate
\[
H(x)=\int_{x^2}^{2x+1}\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int\frac{x}{(1+x^2)^3}\,dx.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int x^2\ln x\,dx.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx.
\]
\item Evaluate
\[
\int\frac{dx}{x^2+9}.
\]
State the substitution or standard form you use.
\item Use the trapezoidal rule with \(n=4\) to estimate
\[
\int_0^2x^3\,dx.
\]
\item Determine whether
\[
\int_0^1x^{-2/3}\,dx
\]
converges. If it converges, find its value.
\item Explain why \(+C\) belongs on an indefinite integral but not on a completed definite-integral evaluation.
\item For each integral, name the best first method and justify the choice in one sentence:
\[
\int x\ln x\,dx,
\qquad
\int\frac{2x}{x^2+7}\,dx,
\qquad
\int\frac{dx}{x^2-4}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

\section{Practice Exam B Answer Key}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\[
6\sqrt{x}+4e^x-5\sin x+C.
\]
\item \(\Delta x=\tfrac12\), with right endpoints \(\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,2\):
\[
R_4=\frac12\left(\frac14+1+\frac94+4\right)=\frac{15}{4}.
\]
\item
\[
f_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac13\int_0^3(x^2+1)dx
=\frac13\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x\right]_0^3=4.
\]
\item Apply FTC to both bounds:
\[
H'(x)=2\sqrt{1+(2x+1)^4}-2x\sqrt{1+x^8}.
\]
\item Let \(u=1+x^2\):
\[
\int\frac{x}{(1+x^2)^3}dx
=\frac12\int u^{-3}du
=-\frac{1}{4(1+x^2)^2}+C.
\]
\item Integration by parts gives
\[
\int x^2\ln x\,dx
=\frac{x^3}{3}\ln x-\frac{x^3}{9}+C.
\]
\item Write \(\sin^3x=(1-\cos^2x)\sin x\) and use \(u=\cos x\):
\[
-\frac{\cos^3x}{3}+\frac{\cos^5x}{5}+C.
\]
\item Using \(x=3\tan\theta\), or the standard arctangent form,
\[
\int\frac{dx}{x^2+9}=\frac13\arctan\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C.
\]
\item With \(h=\tfrac12\),
\[
T_4=\frac{h}{2}\left[f(0)+2f(0.5)+2f(1)+2f(1.5)+f(2)\right]
=\frac{17}{4}.
\]
\item
\[
\int_0^1x^{-2/3}dx
=\lim_{a\to0^+}\left[3x^{1/3}\right]_a^1=3.
\]
The integral converges.
\item Indefinite integration reverses differentiation and therefore determines a family differing by constants. Definite integration subtracts endpoint values, so any antiderivative constant cancels.
\item Use integration by parts for \(\int x\ln x\,dx\); substitution \(u=x^2+7\) for \(\int 2x/(x^2+7)dx\); and partial fractions after factoring \(x^2-4\) for \(\int dx/(x^2-4)\).
\end{enumerate}
